entities.name: Ibn Manda
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Abū ʿAbdullāh Muḥammad bin Isḥāq Ibn Manda (d. 1005 CE) was a pivotal Isfahani Sunni Hadith scholar of Persian lineage, whose extensive travels and rigorous methodology profoundly shaped the transmission and authentication of prophetic traditions in the Islamic world during the late 10th and early 11th centuries. Operating within the intellectual ferment of the Abbasid Caliphate's waning political power but flourishing scholarly culture, Ibn Manda dedicated his life to preserving and systematizing the corpus of Hadith, becoming a leading authority in a field central to Islamic law and theology. His work represents a crucial link in the chain of Hadith transmission, connecting earlier generations of scholars to the encyclopedic compilations that would define Sunni orthodoxy.

Born into a prominent family of Hadith scholars in Isfahan, Persia, Ibn Manda embarked on an epic intellectual journey spanning nearly three decades, traveling across the Islamic heartlands from Transoxiana to Egypt and Mecca between 928 and 958 CE. During this period, he studied under an estimated 1,700 shaykhs and collected an immense number of Hadith, meticulously documenting their chains of transmission (isnād) and scrutinizing their authenticity. His major contributions include monumental works such as 'Kitāb al-Īmān' (Book of Faith), a comprehensive theological treatise, and 'Maʿrifat al-Ṣaḥāba' (Knowledge of the Companions), a biographical dictionary of the Prophet Muhammad's companions, which became foundational texts for subsequent generations of scholars. He also produced significant works on the attributes of God and the history of Isfahan.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Ibn Manda was a leading Hadith scholar whose extensive travels and monumental compilations, such as 'Kitāb al-Īmān', became foundational texts for Sunni Islam. His rigorous methodology influenced generations of scholars, significantly shaping the standards for Hadith authentication and contributing to the intellectual edifice of Islamic jurisprudence and theology.
